Jan Utenhove
yahn ū'ten-hō-vā
n. (Jan Utenhove, c. 1516–1566, Flemish nobleman, elder of the Dutch Church of London, translator of the Dutch New Testament and Psalms)
Dutch Jan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Utenhove, from the court, of a patrician house of Ghent.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jan Utenhove was a patrician of Ghent who left the Netherlands in 1544 for the faith and spent the rest of his life among the exiles, in Strasbourg, London, Emden and Poland. He was never ordained; he served the Dutch Church of London as an elder, and his work was the people's singing and the people's Bible. He put the Psalms into Dutch metre, published in instalments from 1551, which gave the Dutch Reformed their first metrical psalter and were sung in the churches of the Netherlands for a generation; and he translated the whole New Testament into Dutch from the Greek, printed at Emden in 1556, the first Dutch New Testament made from the original. He also wrote the history of the 1553 voyage of the exiles, the fullest account of it. He died in London in 1566, an elder to the last. The two things he gave his people were a Testament they could read and psalms they could sing. “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms, and metre as the measured arrangement of syllables in verse.

expand to see more

PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a psalm-book for singing.

ME'TRE, n. The arrangement of a certain number of syllables in a certain order; measure; verse.

EL'DER, n. In the primitive church, one who had the oversight and care of a church.

MEL'ODY, n. An agreeable succession of sounds; a tune.

Key Scripture

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;"

Psa 95:1 — "O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation."

Psa 104:33 — "I will sing unto the LORD as long as I live: I will sing praise to my God while I have my being."

Jam 5:13 — "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms."

Modern Corruption

The elder who gave the Dutch their first metrical psalter and their first Greek-based Testament.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a modern condescension toward metrical psalmody as a crude expedient of an age without hymns. Utenhove's psalters were not a makeshift. They were an attempt to put the inspired songbook of the church into the mouths of farmers and weavers in their own measure, and the congregations that learned them sang their way through Alva's terror.

The principle to recover is that congregational singing is commanded and that its matter is given: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19). James makes it the ordinary outlet of a settled heart as prayer is of an afflicted one — “Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jam 5:13) — and the psalmist sets the term of the obligation: “I will sing unto the LORD as long as I live” (Psa 104:33).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek psalmos (G5568), a psalm; psallo (G5567), to pluck, sing praise.

expand to see more

Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song sung to an instrument; Ephesians 5:19.

Greek psallo (G5567) — to pluck, to sing praise; Ephesians 5:19.

Greek humnos (G5215) — a hymn, a song of praise; Ephesians 5:19.

Hebrew rua (H7321) — to shout, make a joyful noise; Psalm 95:1.

Hebrew zamar (H2167) — to make music, sing praise; Psalm 104:33.

Usage

"“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19) — the Dutch psalter of 1551."

"“O come, let us sing unto the LORD” (Psa 95:1) — put into Dutch measure."

"“Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jam 5:13) — what the exiles did at sea."
